Square packing with O⁡(x0.6)O(x^{0.6}) wasted area

Hong Duc Bui Email: buihd@u.nus.edu
Abstract

We show a new construction for square packing, and prove that it is more efficient than previous results.

1 Introduction

Square packing is a well-studied problem. Formally, we consider a large square SS with side length xx and ask what is the maximum number of unit squares that can be packed without overlap into SS.

We define W⁡(x)W(x) to be the area of wasted space when a square of side length xx is packed with unit squares. In other words, W⁡(x)W(x) is x2x^{2} minus the maximum number of unit squares that can fit in. (For convenience, our definition of W⁡(x)W(x) is the same as in Erdős and Graham (1975); Chung and Graham (2009); Wang et al. (2016).)

In this article, we are concerned with the behavior of W⁡(x)W(x) as x→∞x\to\infty.

The trivial packing method allows ⌊x⌋2\lfloor x\rfloor^{2} squares to fit in, which shows W⁡(x)≤x2−⌊x⌋2∈O⁡(x)W(x)\leq x^{2}-\lfloor x\rfloor^{2}\in O(x). However, a long line of research Erdős and Graham (1975); Chung and Graham (2009); Wang et al. (2016) has given much better bounds, the best one gives W⁡(x)∈O⁡(x0.625)W(x)\in O(x^{0.625}). Also, Chung and Graham (2019) claims W⁡(x)∈O⁡(x0.6)W(x)\in O(x^{0.6}), but Arslanov and Bui (2025) shows that there is a technical error in the calculation of W5W_{5}, with W5W_{5} defined on (Chung and Graham, 2019, p. 8).

This article extends the insights in Wang et al. (2016) to improve the result, namely W⁡(x)∈O⁡(x0.6)W(x)\in O(x^{0.6}).

On the opposite direction, Roth and Vaughan (1978) proved W⁡(x)∉o⁡(x1/2)W(x)\notin o(x^{1/2}). This is a lower bound on W⁡(x)W(x). Note that W⁡(x)∉Ω⁡(x1/2)W(x)\notin\Omega(x^{1/2}), as W⁡(x)=0W(x)=0 for all positive integer xx.

In a high level, the packing is done as follows. First, packing a square is reduced to packing a right trapezoid, this reduction is described in Section 5. Then, the trapezoid is packed by a certain kind of quadrilateral, this reduction is described in Section 4. Finally, Section 3 describes how to pack such a quadrilateral.

Within these three steps, Section 3 is the most technical, Section 4 is less technical, and Section 5 is standard, and the idea already appear in prior works.

1.1 Note on independent discovery

After putting this manuscript on arXiv, we learnt that an equivalent result was independently discovered by McClenagan McClenagan (Master’s Thesis); McClenagan (2026), with a somewhat different method.

The two methods can be compared as follows.

The “second packing algorithm” in (McClenagan, 2026, Section 3) is similar to the packing method in Section 3, except that it is specialized to have Δ1+Δ2=1\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}=1, so ij=ji_{j}=j for every jj. In particular, im=mi_{m}=m, that is, the packing has the same number of rows as columns.

By only analyzing the case where im=mi_{m}=m, the analysis of wasted area becomes significantly simpler. For comparison, in our article, in the application of Section 3 in Section 4, we only use the case where im∈Θ⁡(m)i_{m}\in\Theta(m). On the other hand, by analyzing the general case where no restriction between imi_{m} and mm are imposed, we allow for more flexibility on the method in Section 4. In particular, we don’t need to use and analyze the dual packing method. Besides, by analyzing the general case, we were able to analyze in Section 6.3 why having im∈Θ⁡(m)i_{m}\in\Theta(m) appear to be the best choice with this packing method.

The “first packing algorithm” in (McClenagan, 2026, Section 2) is a vertical reflection of the so-called dual packing method we briefly mentioned in Section 6.2.

The method used to pack a right trapezoid in Section 4 of our article and (McClenagan, 2026, Section 4) are completely different, as explained above.

The reduction from packing a square and packing a right trapezoid in Section 5 of our article and (McClenagan, 2026, Section 4) are the same, and the same as prior works.

2 Summary of Existing Techniques

The fundamental method used to overcome the trivial bound x2−⌊x⌋2x^{2}-\lfloor x\rfloor^{2} is the following.

Consider two parallel lines at a distance xx apart, we wish to pack the space between them with unit squares. If the trivial packing method is used as in Figure 1, we would get Ω⁡(x−⌊x⌋)\Omega(x-\lfloor x\rfloor) area of wasted space per unit distance. However, if we take vertical stacks of ⌈x⌉\lceil x\rceil unit squares and tilt them as little as possible such that they fit between the two lines, the angle of rotation needed will be O(x−1/2)O(x^{-1/2}), therefore the wasted area is only O(x−1/2)O(x^{-1/2}) per unit distance. See Figure 2 for an illustration.

More generally, the height of each vertical stack can be any integer m≥xm\geq x such that m−x∈O⁡(1)m-x\in O(1). On a first-order approximation, the angle of rotation is usually 2​(m−x)x\sqrt{\frac{2(m-x)}{x}}, as can be computed by an application of Pythagorean theorem.

This result can be interpreted as follows: it provides a family of parallelograms that can be packed with small waste. These parallelograms can then be assembled together to pack a larger shape.

The reason why this is so commonly used Erdős and Graham (1975); Chung and Graham (2009); Wang et al. (2016) is that the parallelogram can have arbitrary (possibly nonintegral) height xx, which allows us to eliminate one obstruction in square packing—two parallel or almost-parallel sides with distance xx apart where xx is not an integer. Unfortunately, it creates another obstruction: the other side of the parallelogram is not perfectly vertical or horizontal.

Previously, there was no good way around this: for example, (Chung and Graham, 2009, Figure 9) cuts away small triangles (denoted eie_{i} in that article) from the side of the slanted trapezoid in order to make the two sides parallel.

In Section 3, we will describe another family of quadrilaterals that can be packed similarly tightly (wasted area == perimeter ×\times slope angle), but have two opposite sides non-parallel. This is the main primitive that we assemble together for the final packing.

3 A Primitive Tightly-packed Quadrilateral

In this section, we prove the existence of a family of quadrilaterals with the following properties:

  • •

    Each interior angle is 90∘±o⁡(1)90^{\circ}\pm o(1). Intuitively, the quadrilateral looks almost like a rectangle (unless the side length is too large, see Section 6.6).

  • •

    Consider one such quadrilateral. It is approximately an axis-aligned rectangle, as above. Let mm and imi_{m} be some positive integers such that the almost-horizontal sides have length ≈m\approx m, the almost-vertical sides have length ≈im\approx i_{m}. Let θ>0\theta>0 such that the top left interior angle has measure 90∘−θ90^{\circ}-\theta.

    Then there is a packing of the quadrilateral with total wasted area ∈O⁡((m+im)​θ)\in O((m+i_{m})\theta).

  • •

    This packing uses only almost-axis-aligned unit squares, that is, each unit square can be rotated by an angle of o⁡(1)o(1) to become perfectly axis-aligned.

The whole packing is illustrated in Figure 8, where the quadrilateral to be packed is A​B​C​DABCD.

We would like to note that this packing method is inspired from Wang et al. (2016). The connection is described in Section 6.5.

Furthermore, when im∈Θ⁡(m)i_{m}\in\Theta(m), our packing method has the asymptotically smallest wasted area among all packings for this family of quadrilaterals. This is shown in Section 3.3.

For the convenience of the reader, all notations used in this section are listed in Table 1. Some of the notations (in particular, θ\theta, σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2}) are used again in later chapters.

Remark 3.3.

There is an alternative way to calculate the wasted area: count the number of squares, then subtract that from the area of the trapezoid A​B​C​DABCD.

Clearly the number of squares (including Sim,mS_{i_{m},m}) is m⋅imm\cdot i_{m}. If we can show that the area of the trapezoid A​B​C​DABCD is ≤m⋅im+O⁡(θ⋅(m+im)+1)\leq m\cdot i_{m}+O(\theta\cdot(m+i_{m})+1), we would be able to conclude that the total wasted area is O⁡(θ⋅(m+im)+1)O(\theta\cdot(m+i_{m})+1).

Calculating the area of the trapezoid A​B​C​DABCD appears to be difficult. See Appendix A.

3.3 Lower Bound on the Wasted Area

As mentioned in Section 2, the existing method for packing the area between two parallel lines a distance xx apart can be interpreted as giving an efficient packing method for a family of parallelograms. We illustrate such a parallelogram in Figure 11.

If we have to pack the interior of such a parallelogram, this packing method is in fact asymptotically optimal in certain cases.

Proposition 3.4.

Consider a parallelogram that can be perfectly packed by the method illustrated in Figure 11. Let xx be its height. Suppose ⌈x⌉−x∈Θ⁡(1)\lceil x\rceil-x\in\Theta(1) and the width of the parallelogram is ∈Θ⁡(x)\in\Theta(x). Then the internal angle of the parallelogram is 90∘±Θ⁡(1/x)90^{\circ}\pm\Theta(1/\sqrt{x}), and the packing method has wasted area Θ⁡(x)\Theta(\sqrt{x}).

Proof 3.5.

Suppose the horizontal edge is parallel to the xx-axis. Let θ\theta be the tilt of the almost-vertical edge, and w∈Θ⁡(x)w\in\Theta(x) be the number of almost-vertical stack of squares illustrated in Figure 11. Then, the wasted area consists of 2​w2w small triangles, each have area 12​tan⁡θ\frac{1}{2}\tan\theta. Therefore, the total wasted area is w​tan⁡θ∈Θ⁡(x​θ)w\tan\theta\in\Theta(x\theta). An easy calculation shows that if ⌈x⌉−x∈Θ⁡(1)\lceil x\rceil-x\in\Theta(1) then θ∈Θ⁡(1/x)\theta\in\Theta(1/\sqrt{x}).

Proposition 3.6.

A parallelogram with height xx, width Θ⁡(x)\Theta(x), and internal angle 90∘±θ90^{\circ}\pm\theta for θ∈Θ⁡(1/x)\theta\in\Theta(1/\sqrt{x}) has the minimum wasted area of a packing with unit squares Ω⁡(x)\Omega(\sqrt{x}).

The following is a more formal version of the statement of Proposition 3.6. For all functions w1​(x),w2​(x)∈Θ⁡(x)w_{1}(x),w_{2}(x)\in\Theta(x), θ1​(x),θ2​(x)∈Θ⁡(1/x)\theta_{1}(x),\theta_{2}(x)\in\Theta(1/\sqrt{x}), there exists a function a⁡(x)∈Ω⁡(x)a(x)\in\Omega(\sqrt{x}) such that for any parallelogram with height xx, width between w1​(x)w_{1}(x) and w2​(x)w_{2}(x), and one internal angle 90∘+θ90^{\circ}+\theta for θ1​(x)≤θ≤θ2​(x)\theta_{1}(x)\leq\theta\leq\theta_{2}(x) the minimum wasted area of a packing of that parallelogram is ≥a⁡(x)\geq a(x).

Proof 3.7.

We prove that any packing requires wasted area ∈Ω⁡(x​θ)\in\Omega(x\theta). Pick Θ⁡(x)\Theta(x) equidistant points each along the left and bottom edge of the parallelogram, and connect the corresponding points, getting Θ⁡(x)\Theta(x) parallel line segments. This is depicted with red downwards-sloping line segments in Figure 11. Let these paths be γ1\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2}, …\dots, γk\gamma_{k} with k∈Θ⁡(x)k\in\Theta(x).

Because the width and the height of the parallelogram are both Θ⁡(x)\Theta(x), the paths are at a distance Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) apart. Using (Bui, 2025, Proposition 21) (with minor adaptation to make it work with two sides of the boundary instead of two unit squares) on each of the paths γ1\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2}, …\dots, γk\gamma_{k}, because the left and bottom edges are sloped by θ\theta with respect to each other, for each such path, the total wasted area in a region near each path is ∈Ω⁡(θ)\in\Omega(\theta). Since the kk paths are at distance Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) apart, each point is only near O⁡(1)O(1) paths, therefore the total wasted area in any packing of the parallelogram is ∈Ω⁡(k​θ)=Ω⁡(x​θ)\in\Omega(k\theta)=\Omega(x\theta), finishing the proof.

Using a very similar argument, we can see that when m/im∈Θ⁡(1)m/i_{m}\in\Theta(1), a quadrilateral with almost-vertical and almost-horizontal sides with width Θ⁡(m)\Theta(m), height Θ⁡(im)\Theta(i_{m}), and an interior angle 90∘−Θ⁡(θ)90^{\circ}-\Theta(\theta) must have wasted area Ω⁡((m+im)⋅θ)\Omega((m+i_{m})\cdot\theta). Therefore, for the quadrilaterals formed by our packing method described in this section, our method is asymptotically optimal up to a multiplicative constant factor.

4 Packing a Right Trapezoid

We consider a right trapezoid with height xx, base Θ⁡(xβ)\Theta(x^{\beta}), slope of right edge Θ⁡(x−γ)\Theta(x^{-\gamma}), where β\beta and γ\gamma are some positive constants. We will describe a packing method that results in the wasted area being Θ⁡(x1−γ/2)\Theta(x^{1-\gamma/2}) under some choices of β\beta and γ\gamma.

This packing method is illustrated in Figure 12. Informally, we first pack the cyan quadrilateral E0​G0​M0​N0E_{0}G_{0}M_{0}N_{0} with the method in Section 3, leave a gap N0​M0​G1​E1N_{0}M_{0}G_{1}E_{1} with integral height that can be almost perfectly packed and segment E1​G1E_{1}G_{1} has length slightly more than an integer, which allows us to continue packing the cyan quadrilateral E1​G1​M1​N1E_{1}G_{1}M_{1}N_{1} with the same method in Section 3. In doing so, the edge M0​N0M_{0}N_{0}, and thus E1​G1E_{1}G_{1}, is slightly more tilted than E0​G0E_{0}G_{0}. Similarly, E2​G2E_{2}G_{2} is slightly more tilted than E1​G1E_{1}G_{1}, etc.

Later, we will specialize to γ=12\gamma=\frac{1}{2} and β=1−γ2=34\beta=1-\frac{\gamma}{2}=\frac{3}{4}. All notations used in this section are listed in Table 2.

4.1 Details of the Packing Method

We perform the following procedure. See Figure 12 for demonstration.

First, define ω=γ2\omega=\frac{\gamma}{2} and pick θ∈Θ⁡(x−ω)\theta\in\Theta(x^{-\omega}), the exact constant factor to be decided later. Then pick E0E_{0} on segment A​DAD, its exact position to be determined later. Pick G0G_{0} on segment B​CBC such that the angle A​E0​G0AE_{0}G_{0} is (90+θ)∘(90+\theta)^{\circ}.

Proposition 4.8.

The set of locations of E0E_{0} on segment A​DAD such that segment E0​G0E_{0}G_{0} has length tan⁡θ\tan\theta more than an integer is a discrete set of points, each Θ⁡(xγ)\Theta(x^{\gamma}) spaced apart from its nearest neighbor.

This comes immediately from the fact that line B​CBC makes with line A​DAD an angle of Θ⁡(x−γ)\Theta(x^{-\gamma}). Therefore, there exists a choice of E0E_{0} such that segment A​E0AE_{0} has length Θ⁡(xγ)\Theta(x^{\gamma}).

Using this choice of E0E_{0}, construct a tightly-packed quadrilateral (as described in Section 3) right below segment E0​G0E_{0}G_{0}. Let the two bottom vertices of it be M0M_{0} and N0N_{0} respectively, with M0M_{0} on B​CBC and N0N_{0} on A​DAD.

Let θ\theta, σ1\sigma_{1}, σ2\sigma_{2} be as in Section 3, where we use quadrilateral E0​G0​M0​N0E_{0}G_{0}M_{0}N_{0} here in place of the quadrilateral A​B​C​DABCD in Section 3. Notice that the θ\theta as in Section 3 agrees with our definition of θ\theta at the start of this section, and σ1∈Θ⁡(x−γ)\sigma_{1}\in\Theta(x^{-\gamma}) is the slope of the right edge.

Then, define θ1\theta_{1} to be the angle that N0​M0N_{0}M_{0} makes with the horizontal line. We have θ1=θ+σ2\theta_{1}=\theta+\sigma_{2}.

We will construct points E1E_{1} and G1G_{1} on segments N0​DN_{0}D and B​CBC respectively such that E1​G1E_{1}G_{1} is parallel to N0​M0N_{0}M_{0}.

Arguing similar to Proposition 4.8, the set of possible locations of E1E_{1} such that the length of E1​G1E_{1}G_{1} is tan⁡θ1\tan\theta_{1} more than an integer is a discrete set of points, each Θ⁡(xγ)\Theta(x^{\gamma}) spaced apart from its nearest neighbor. Thus we can pick E1E_{1} being one of those points such that segment N0​E1N_{0}E_{1} has length Θ⁡(xγ)\Theta(x^{\gamma}).

Move E1E_{1} slightly downwards (by a length of O⁡(1)O(1)) so that the segment N0​E1N_{0}E_{1} has integral length. Move G1G_{1} accordingly, keeping E1​G1E_{1}G_{1} parallel to N0​M0N_{0}M_{0}.

Construct a quadrilateral E1​G1​M1​N1E_{1}G_{1}M_{1}N_{1} similar to above. Because of the movement of E1E_{1} above, we might have to trim away a vertical strip of height approximately E1​N1E_{1}N_{1} and width O⁡(x−γ)O(x^{-\gamma}) from the left side of the quadrilateral, near segment E1​N1E_{1}N_{1}. Since the height of the right trapezoid is xx, the total wasted area caused by this trimming is O⁡(x1−γ)O(x^{1-\gamma}). This is asymptotically smaller than the Θ⁡(x1−γ/2)\Theta(x^{1-\gamma/2}) that will be shown later, thus can be safely ignored.

Then, keep constructing quadrilaterals {Ei​Gi​Mi​Ni}i\{E_{i}G_{i}M_{i}N_{i}\}_{i} following the same procedure until the bottom edge is reached. Let kk be the maximum integer for which the quadrilateral Ek​Gk​Mk​NkE_{k}G_{k}M_{k}N_{k} was constructed and entirely contained in the right trapezoid A​B​C​DABCD.

Next, for each gap Ni​Mi​Gi+1​Ei+1N_{i}M_{i}G_{i+1}E_{i+1}, we fill it with vertical stacks of unit squares with height equal to the length of segment N0​E1N_{0}E_{1}. An illustration is in Figure 13.

Note that there is some overlap with the region above N0​M0N_{0}M_{0}, but this is fine—recall the construction in Section 3, these columns merely extends the T∙,jT_{\bullet,j} columns. The right end near M0​G1M_{0}G_{1} is sloped, they can be filled in naively.

The top and bottom part can be filled in naively with waste proportional to the total perimeter of quadrilaterals A​B​G0​E0ABG_{0}E_{0} and Nk​Mk​C​DN_{k}M_{k}CD.

First, we consider the quadrilateral E0​G0​M0​N0E_{0}G_{0}M_{0}N_{0}. We use the notation θ\theta, σ1\sigma_{1}, σ2\sigma_{2}, mm and imi_{m} for width and height as in Section 3.

We have shown that we need no more than ⌈l4​d3​xω⌉\bigl\lceil\frac{l}{4d^{3}}x^{\omega}\bigr\rceil quadrilaterals to fill the whole trapezoid A​B​C​DABCD, and the first ⌈l4​d3​xω⌉\bigl\lceil\frac{l}{4d^{3}}x^{\omega}\bigr\rceil quadrilaterals have θi∈Ω⁡(x−ω)\theta_{i}\in\Omega(x^{-\omega}), so Proposition 4.11 is proven.

Next, we analyze the wasted area.

The top and bottom part have wasted area O⁡(xβ+xγ)O(x^{\beta}+x^{\gamma}).

There are O⁡(x1−max⁡(β,γ))O(x^{1-\max(\beta,\gamma)}) such quadrilaterals, and roughly as many gaps. For each quadrilateral, the waste is O⁡((m+im)​θ)=O⁡(xβ−ω)O((m+i_{m})\theta)=O(x^{\beta-\omega}). O⁡(xβ+xγ+x1−max⁡(β,γ)⋅(xβ−γ/2+xγ)).O\bigl(x^{\beta}+x^{\gamma}+x^{1-\max(\beta,\gamma)}\cdot(x^{\beta-\gamma/2}+x^{\gamma})\bigr).

5 Reduction from Packing a Square to Packing a Right Trapezoid

We will state a proposition which describes a packing method that allows one to reduces the problem of packing a square to the problem of packing a right trapezoid, special cases of which has already been used several times in previous works.

Define Wβ,ϵ​(x)=x2​β2​β+1​logϵ2​β+1​xW_{\beta,\epsilon}(x)=x^{\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+1}}\log^{\frac{\epsilon}{2\beta+1}}x. We would like to note that 2​β2​β+1\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+1} is the harmonic mean of 12\frac{1}{2} and β\beta.

Proposition 5.19.

If there exists real 12<β<1\frac{1}{2}<\beta<1, real 0<ν<β+120<\nu<\beta+\frac{1}{2}, real ϵ\epsilon such that for all real mm, for all w∈Θ⁡(mν)w\in\Theta(m^{\nu}), the right trapezoid with height mm, smaller base ww, larger base w+Θ⁡(m)w+\Theta(\sqrt{m}) can be packed with wasted area O⁡(mβ​logϵ​m)O(m^{\beta}\log^{\epsilon}m), then W⁡(x)∈O⁡(Wβ,ϵ​(x))W(x)\in O(W_{\beta,\epsilon}(x)).

This trapezoid is roughly the same as a “type 2” shape in Chung and Graham (2009); Wang et al. (2016), except that we make the constant factor implicit rather than explicit.

The wasted area is O⁡(mβ​logϵ​m+xm)O(m^{\beta}\log^{\epsilon}m+\frac{x}{\sqrt{m}}). By selecting m=(x​log−ϵ​x)22​β+1m=(x\log^{-\epsilon}x)^{\frac{2}{2\beta+1}}, the quantity above is minimized, being O⁡(x2​β2​β+1​logϵ2​β+1​x)=Wβ,ϵ​(x)O(x^{\frac{2\beta}{2\beta+1}}\log^{\frac{\epsilon}{2\beta+1}}x)=W_{\beta,\epsilon}(x).

Note that ν\nu cannot be too large otherwise it may happen that mν>xm^{\nu}>x.

We see this being applied in previous results as follows. Note that 4−27<1\frac{4-\sqrt{2}}{7}<1.

Article mβ​logϵ​mm^{\beta}\log^{\epsilon}m Choice of mm Wβ,ϵ​(x)W_{\beta,\epsilon}(x)
Erdős and Graham (1975) m7/8m^{7/8} x8/11x^{8/11} x7/11x^{7/11}
Chung and Graham (2009) m2+24​log⁡mm^{\frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{4}}\log m x2−2​αx^{2-2\alpha}, with α=3+27\alpha=\frac{3+\sqrt{2}}{7} x3+27​log4−27​xx^{\frac{3+\sqrt{2}}{7}}\log^{\frac{4-\sqrt{2}}{7}}x

In this article, when β=34\beta=\frac{3}{4}, we get:

Theorem 5.20.

W⁡(x)∈O⁡(x3/5)W(x)\in O(x^{3/5}).

That proves the claim in the introduction.

6 Discussion

6.1 Symmetry of the Construction

We discuss a symmetry in the construction described in Section 3.

Note that if we shift each T∙,jT_{\bullet,j} stack down until they touch segment C​DCD, the small rectangles in W6W_{6} will disappear, instead, some small rectangles will appear above the stacks T∙,jT_{\bullet,j}—and we see the symmetry of the construction between W1↔W3W_{1}\leftrightarrow W_{3}, W2↔W6W_{2}\leftrightarrow W_{6}, W4↔W5W_{4}\leftrightarrow W_{5}, σ1↔σ2\sigma_{1}\leftrightarrow\sigma_{2}, S↔TS\leftrightarrow T.

The symmetry is also shown in the following formula that relates θ\theta, σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2}:

sec(θ+σ1)sinσ1⋅sec(θ+σ2)sinσ2=(1−cosθ)2.\sec(\theta+\sigma_{1})\sin\sigma_{1}\cdot\sec(\theta+\sigma_{2})\sin\sigma_{2}=(1-\cos\theta)^{2}.

And the following formula (this can be derived from im≈θ22​σ1​mi_{m}\approx\frac{\theta^{2}}{2\sigma_{1}}m):

imσ2≈mσ1.\frac{i_{m}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{2}}}\approx\frac{m}{\sqrt{\sigma_{1}}}.

While the square root may look weird, a better way to look at it is the following: if θ\theta and mm are fixed, in order to double σ2\sigma_{2}, you need to multiply imi_{m} by roughly the same factor 22. In formula: im≈2​σ2θ2​mi_{m}\approx\frac{2\sigma_{2}}{\theta^{2}}m.

Note that the area of W6W_{6} does not have a O⁡(σ2​m)O(\sigma_{2}m) term likely because our analysis is not exactly symmetric, in particular the width of W2W_{2} is measured being perpendicular to A​DAD but the height of W6W_{6} is measured being parallel to A​DAD instead of perpendicular to A​BAB. Nevertheless, the result is not affected.

6.2 Dual of the Packing Method

We would like to note that there is a natural dual to the method in Section 3. See Figure 14.

Here, the horizontal stacks are angled upwards instead of downwards, and it is necessary that θ>σ1\theta>\sigma_{1}. We don’t analyze this configuration because it appears to be not particularly useful.

6.3 Limitation of the Packing Method

Consider the packing method in Section 4. Suppose we choose some value of ω\omega different from γ2\frac{\gamma}{2}.

If ω<γ2\omega<\frac{\gamma}{2}, then θ>x−γ/2\theta>x^{-\gamma/2} for large enough xx, then the waste comes from the quadrilaterals alone is ≥Ω⁡(x⋅θ)\geq\Omega(x\cdot\theta) which is more than x1−γ/2x^{1-\gamma/2}.

If ω>γ2\omega>\frac{\gamma}{2}, the height of each quadrilateral is Θ⁡(xβ+γ−2​ω)\Theta(x^{\beta+\gamma-2\omega}) which is much less than the width Θ⁡(xβ)\Theta(x^{\beta}). Consequently, the total perimeter of the quadrilaterals is much more than the sum of the heights. Assume at least a constant factor of the height comes from the quadrilaterals instead of the gaps (that is β+γ−2​ω≥γ\beta+\gamma-2\omega\geq\gamma), then the wasted area (again comes from the quadrilaterals alone) is Θ⁡(x2​ω−γ⋅x⋅θ)=Θ⁡(x1+ω−γ)\Theta(x^{2\omega-\gamma}\cdot x\cdot\theta)=\Theta(x^{1+\omega-\gamma}), and 1+ω−γ>1−γ21+\omega-\gamma>1-\frac{\gamma}{2}.

As such, it appears that Ω⁡(x1−γ/2)\Omega(x^{1-\gamma/2}) is a natural lower bound for our method. And, with β=12\beta=\frac{1}{2}, our method of packing naively the top/bottom/right side area in Section 4 does not hurt us, since naive packing already gives O⁡(x1−γ/2)O(x^{1-\gamma/2}).

There is another interpretation for Ω⁡(x1−γ/2)\Omega(x^{1-\gamma/2}). Consider Figure 15. If the trapezoid A​B​C​DABCD is subdivided into smaller right trapezoids by cutting horizontally, such that each triangle formed by drawing a vertical line from the top right corner to the bottom edge has area Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) (colored cyan in the figure), then you need Θ⁡(x1−θ/2)\Theta(x^{1-\theta/2}) such triangles. It appears unlikely that it is possible to pack each of these small trapezoid with average wasted area o⁡(1)o(1) each.

As such, we make the following conjecture:

Conjecture 6.21.

For 0<γ<10<\gamma<1, a right trapezoid with height xx and difference between two bases Θ⁡(x1−γ)\Theta(x^{1-\gamma}) cannot be packed in o⁡(x1−γ/2)o(x^{1-\gamma/2}).

Unfortunately, the most straightforward method to prove this—proving that each such right trapezoid has wasted area Ω⁡(1)\Omega(1)—doesn’t work (when β>γ>0\beta>\gamma>0), as depicted in the configuration in Figure 16.

We consider the right trapezoid colored gray. Draw a blue diagonal line as in the figure, then draw a yellow line parallel to the bottom side and a red line parallel to the top side. Pack each region with stacks of squares with tilt Θ(x−β/2)\Theta(x^{-\beta/2}).

Then the difference in the xx-coordinate of the two endpoints of the blue diagonal line is Θ⁡(xβ/2)\Theta(x^{\beta/2}), which is larger than the distance Θ⁡(xγ/2)\Theta(x^{\gamma/2}) marked on the figure. The total wasted area inside the gray right trapezoid is then O(xγ/2⋅(x−β/2+x−γ))⊆o(1)O(x^{\gamma/2}\cdot(x^{-\beta/2}+x^{-\gamma}))\subseteq o(1).

Nonetheless, we hope it is possible to adapt the methods in Roth and Vaughan (1978).

However, getting from the x1−γ/2x^{1-\gamma/2} barrier to a better lower bound for square packing is still highly nontrivial, since there is no reason why a packing method must use a reduction of the form Proposition 5.19. See Figure 17 for an illustration.

6.4 Packing Other Shapes

We have shown in Section 4 that for certain values of β\beta and γ\gamma, a right trapezoid with height xx, width Θ⁡(xβ)\Theta(x^{\beta}), slope of right angle Θ⁡(x−γ)\Theta(x^{-\gamma}) can be packed with wasted area Θ⁡(x1−γ)\Theta(x^{1-\gamma}). (Note that, assuming β≥1−γ\beta\geq 1-\gamma, when β\beta is too small, the wasted area is dominated by x1−β/2x^{1-\beta/2}, and when β\beta is too large the wasted area is dominated by xβ−1/2x^{\beta-1/2}.)

Our method as is only works for γ\gamma up to 12\frac{1}{2}. Additional considerations, such as packing the top/bottom/right area of the gap intelligently by recursively using the original method (the method of recursive packing can be found in Chung and Graham (2009)) may make it work for higher γ\gamma. Further research is needed to determine the behavior at various values of γ\gamma.

In fact, we make the following conjecture:

Conjecture 6.22.

For any value β≥0\beta\geq 0 and γ≥0\gamma\geq 0, the optimal exponent in the wasted area asymptotic of packing a trapezoid with height xx, width Θ⁡(xβ)\Theta(x^{\beta}), slope of right angle Θ⁡(x−γ)\Theta(x^{-\gamma}) is

max⁡(1−max⁡(β,1−γ)2,1−γ2,β−12,35).\max\Bigl(1-\frac{\max(\beta,1-\gamma)}{2},1-\frac{\gamma}{2},\beta-\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{5}\Bigr).

The wasted area of the trivial packing method is Θ⁡(x⁡(x−⌊x⌋))\Theta(x(x-\lfloor x\rfloor)), therefore, when x−⌊x⌋∈o(x−2/5)x-\lfloor x\rfloor\in o(x^{-2/5}) then it is possible to get the wasted area o⁡(x3/5)o(x^{3/5}). That poses the question:

Question 6.23.

Is it possible to get wasted area o⁡(x3/5)o(x^{3/5}) when x−⌊x⌋∈Θ(x−2/5)x-\lfloor x\rfloor\in\Theta(x^{-2/5})?

When x−⌊x⌋∈Θ(x−2/5)x-\lfloor x\rfloor\in\Theta(x^{-2/5}), Roth and Vaughan (1978) gives the lower bound x3/10x^{3/10}.

Our reason for focusing on right trapezoid is that the problem of packing arbitrary almost-rectangular quadrilaterals can often be reduced to packing right trapezoids by dividing such quadrilaterals into a small number of right trapezoids. The reduction may not be optimal, however.

6.5 Inspiration for the Primitive Tightly-packed Quadrilateral

Here we explain the connection between Wang et al. (2016) and our construction in Section 3.

In Wang et al. (2016), noticing that the slope of each horizontal stack is roughly 2​δw\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{w}}, when δ\delta changes by a small amount, say w−0.9w^{-0.9}, in order to make 2​δw\frac{2\delta}{w} remains roughly the same, the denominator should be scaled by roughly the same factor as the numerator.

Suppose δ∈Θ⁡(1)\delta\in\Theta(1). Then δ−Θ⁡(w0.1)≈δ⋅(1−Θ⁡(w−0.9))\delta-\Theta(w^{0.1})\approx\delta\cdot(1-\Theta(w^{-0.9})). We want to scale the numerator by the same factor, namely changing the numerator from ww to w⋅(1−Θ⁡(w−0.9))w\cdot(1-\Theta(w^{-0.9})), which is w−Θ⁡(w0.1)w-\Theta(w^{0.1}).

In this article, we made two modifications:

  • •

    we change ww (and thus the slope) gradually, instead of in bulk;

  • •

    we work backward: instead of using δ\delta and the desired slope to determine ww as in Wang et al. (2016), we use the slope of the stack of squares and δ\delta to determine ww. As such, we can ensure the slope difference is exactly zero, at the cost of a small wasted area elsewhere.

6.6 On Packing of Triangle-like Right Trapezoid

Consider a right trapezoid T⁡(x,Θ⁡(xβ),Θ⁡(x−γ))T(x,\Theta(x^{\beta}),\Theta(x^{-\gamma})) where β>0\beta>0 and γ>0\gamma>0. Even though γ>0\gamma>0, it is not necessarily true that the trapezoid will look approximately like a rectangle. This is because the top (smaller) side has length Θ⁡(xβ)\Theta(x^{\beta}), the bottom (larger) side has length Θ⁡(xβ)+Θ⁡(x1−γ)\Theta(x^{\beta})+\Theta(x^{1-\gamma}), if 1−γ>β1-\gamma>\beta, then the right trapezoid in fact looks like a triangle. See Figure 18.

We would like to note that it is possible to split a triangle-like trapezoid to O⁡(log⁡x)O(\log x) right trapezoids, with each of them having bottom side no more than twice the top side. This would allow us to only focus on packing trapezoids with ratio of two bases ∈Θ⁡(1)\in\Theta(1).

In fact, we conjecture the following:

Conjecture 6.24.

The strategy of packing a triangle-like right trapezoid by first subdividing into O⁡(log⁡x)O(\log x) right trapezoids as above, then packing each of them optimally, is asymptotically no worse than the optimal strategy.

7 Conclusion

We have shown that the wasted area when packing a large square with side length xx can be as small as O⁡(x3/5)O(x^{3/5}). Further research is needed to prove or disprove various bounds, such as the bound x1−γ/2x^{1-\gamma/2} pointed out earlier, and extending the result to non-square shapes.
